To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
phosphatidyl-serine (PS), a phospholipid, is required for the activation of RHO1 and PKC1 in Saccharomyce cerevisiae.
phosphatidyl-serine, not diacylglycerol, is the lipid that activates the C1 domain-containing protein kinase C, Pkc1, in the budding yeast, Saccharomycescerevisiae.

PS, not DAG, is the physiological ligand of the Pkc1-C1 domain, and PS plays a role in the activation of Pkc 1 by regulating the localization of the Pkc 1-C1 domain at the bud tip and its interaction with the small G protein Rho1.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of PS in the activation of Pkc signaling.
the mechanism underlying the activation of Pkc signaling in S. cerevisiae.
the mechanism of Pkc1 activation in S. cerevisiae.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
phosphatidyl serine is a key player in the activation of Pkc signaling.
phosphatidyl serine is required for the localization of Pck1 at the bud site and for its physical interaction with GTP bound Rho1.
PS is necessary in Pkc1 activation in vivo.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
PS is a critical lipid for Pkc1 function in S. cerevisiae.
PS plays a role in Pkc1 activation through its role in the localization of Pck1 and its physical interaction with Rho1.
PS is an activator of Rho1-Pkc1 signaling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the C1 domain is not the only membrane-targeting module of Pkc1.
the C1 domain is involved in the activation of Pkc signaling through the interaction of PS and Rho1 in yeast.
phosphatidyl serine is necessary to activate the Rho1-related protein kinase C (Pkc1), a protein that is essential to cell wall integrity in yeast.
